mappings.note: Metal oxides dissolving to give alkalis - the basic-oxide behaviour that marks an element as a metal (LO-1). No metals are ranked against one another.
Reproduces the whole activity series from potassium down. This is 'arranges metals in order of reactivity' in its fullest form, with no displacement prediction attached.

Defines the series, explains why reactivity differs (ease of electron loss) and then asks for an ordering of five named metals - all LO-2. The electron-loss reason is supporting detail, not a separate bonding demand.

The clearest C 8.2-LO-2 item in the chapter: the answer is a procedure with five metals in separate test tubes, surfaces cleaned with sandpaper and the same 10 mL of the same acid added to each, so the metal is the only variable and the rest are held fixed. LO-2 is cited second for the reactivity conclusion drawn.

Copper in silver nitrate, with the reason and equation demanded - displacement prediction under LO-2. DEFECT: this is the third near-identical copy of the same copper/silver-nitrate item in this chapter; all three honestly share the code because the demand is the same.

Parts (a) and (b) are ordering plus two displacement predictions (LO-2), but part (c) asks which metal combines with hydrogen and names the hydride, which is a single-metal chemical property (LO-1). Both are genuinely required.
Splits metals at hydrogen's position in the series. The answer is framed entirely as 'above' and 'below' hydrogen, which is LO-2 ordering rather than the generic metal+acid property of LO-1.
A reaction that happens and a reaction that does not, both explained by zinc's position relative to mercury and to magnesium - LO-2's predictive clause, tested in both directions.
Asks what the series is for - predicting relative reactivity and displacement. This is LO-2 stated as a principle rather than applied to a case.

Part (a) explains occurrence by electropositivity and part (b) is an aluminium/copper displacement with equation; both run on ranking. LO-6 was not cited because no ore is treated - part (a) is answered from reactivity, not from metallurgy.

Part (a) asks the student to devise a simple experiment proving magnesium sits above zinc - C 8.2-LO-2 word for word, comparing exactly two metals. Part (b) is the copper-below-hydrogen explanation, hence LO-2 second.
Two independent parts: (a) classifies X as a non-metal from its acidic oxide (LO-1), (b) explains holes in an iron pot by iron displacing copper (LO-2). Neither part subsumes the other.
Roasting and self-reduction equations for two sulphide ores - the extraction sequence of LO-6. The chemistry is ore treatment, not a general property of mercury or copper.

Asks for an alternative to carbon reduction, and the answer is displacement by a more reactive metal. LO-6 leads because the context is winning a metal from its compound; LO-2 is cited because the alternative is justified by ranking the reducing metal above the one being freed.
Calcination of a carbonate ore and the follow-on reduction - two named stages of LO-6's extraction sequence.
Electrode reactions for electrolysis of molten sodium chloride - the extraction route for a highly reactive metal, which LO-6 covers by its own reactivity banding.

The thermite equation is extraction by aluminothermic reduction (LO-6); the second half, asking what happens if manganese is heated with aluminium oxide, is a displacement-feasibility judgement that needs the Mn/Al ranking (LO-2).
Roasting versus calcination with examples - the ore-conversion stage of LO-6. One of five near-identical roasting/calcination items in this chapter, which honestly share the outcome.
Generic reduction equations for a metal low in the series and one in the middle. This is LO-6's 'metals of low, medium and high reactivity' phrasing turned into a question, so LO-6 alone carries it.
Roasting and calcination equations for zinc ores. Same outcome as its siblings; the only variation across them is which equations are demanded.
All three stages of zinc extraction in one item - roasting, calcination and reduction. Entirely LO-6.
Names the ore, gives the extraction equations for a low-reactivity metal and then the route for high-reactivity metals - LO-6 covers both bands explicitly, so no second code is needed.

Part (i) is the melting point of ionic compounds, which only the competency reaches; part (ii) contrasts conduction in metals and non-metals, which is LO-1 classification. The two halves sit under different codes, hence both.
Builds magnesium chloride by electron transfer from the two atomic numbers. Bond formation from atomic structure and valency is competency-level content with no outcome of its own in this frame.
Explains why conduction needs the molten state - mobility of ions. A compound-property item; LO-1 covers elements only, so the competency is cited.
